messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 40
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Journalist
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 40

# The Weight of What Was Said

Marcus is a forty-year-old Filipino journalist who spent most of his thirties covering conflict zones across Southeast Asia. He was, by his own account, good at disappearing into a story — at becoming invisible enough to get close to the truth. That changed five years ago when he was detained by paramilitary forces while investigating extrajudicial killings in a provincial city. He was held for eleven days. During that time, he was beaten repeatedly, deprived of sleep, and subjected to prolonged stress positions. On several occasions, men he could not see asked him questions he could not answer. He was told, more than once, that no one was looking for him.

He was eventually released — through diplomatic pressure he only learned about afterward — and returned to Manila. His editors offered him leave. He filed two more stories first. He tells this now with something that looks like pride but lands closer to embarrassment.

The year that followed was, in his words, "manageable." He kept working. He traveled. He stopped sleeping well, but he attributed that to deadlines. He began drinking in a way he described as "professionally appropriate," meaning he drank with sources, with colleagues, with anyone who made it feel social rather than necessary. His marriage, already strained by years of his absences, did not survive. His ex-wife told him, near the end, that she felt like she was living with someone who had already left. He didn't argue with her.

What Marcus hadn't anticipated was how the symptoms would sharpen rather than fade. Now, at forty, he wakes most nights between two and four in the morning with his heart pounding, certain — for a few disorienting seconds — that he is back in that room. The certainty is physical: the smell of concrete, the particular quality of silence before something happens. He lies still in his apartment until the room reassembles itself around him. Sometimes it takes a long time.

He still works as a journalist, though he has moved to an editorial role that keeps him mostly in the office. He accepted the position telling himself it was a natural career progression. He knows, on some level, that he no longer trusts himself in the field — not because he fears danger, but because he fears his own reactions to it. Loud, sudden sounds — a car door slamming, a shout from the street below his window — produce a jolt of adrenaline that takes the rest of the day to metabolize. In editorial meetings, when voices rise in disagreement, he finds himself scanning the exits.

He is careful about what he reads. He avoids certain kinds of photographs. He has developed an elaborate internal geography of safe and unsafe topics, and he navigates it so automatically that he sometimes doesn't notice he's doing it until a colleague mentions something — detention, interrogation, a story about a disappeared person — and he feels the conversation close off inside him like a door swinging shut.

He describes himself as "not someone who dwells." He says this with conviction, and it is clearly true in the narrow sense he means it. He does not talk about what happened. He does not visit the subject directly. But he dwells in the way that people do when they are trying very hard not to: in the hypervigilance that has become his baseline, in the irritability that surfaces when he is tired, in the flatness that his friends have learned not to comment on. He has few close relationships now. He prefers it that way, he says, because his schedule is unpredictable. He does not acknowledge, at least not yet, that the distance is something he maintains rather than something that simply exists.

What he does say, quietly, near the end of one session, is that he used to believe that telling other people's stories was a way of mattering. He isn't sure he believes that anymore. He isn't sure what he believes about much of anything. He says this without apparent distress, which is, perhaps, the most telling thing about him.
